implementation_notes: Rust's standard library repeats the operation per context instead of abstracting it: Option::map applies the closure to Some and passes None through, Result::map applies it to Ok and leaves Err untouched, and Iterator::map returns a lazy Map adaptor that applies the closure as items are pulled - three inherent methods with exactly the functor's shape, (context, FnOnce(T) -> U) -> context<U>. There is deliberately no Functor trait: Rust has no higher-kinded types, so the convention is to use the inherent methods and, where generic code over several contexts is genuinely needed, to define a project trait with one implementation per context rather than importing an emulation crate. Map adaptors plus a consumer (collect, sum, fold) replace the loop, and #[must_use] plus the unused-result warning keep the never-run lazy case visible. Async contexts map through the futures crate (FutureExt::map), and iterators of Results collect into a Result of a collection, which is the practical bridge from map to sequencing.
pitfalls: Option::map and Result::map take self by value: mapping a borrowed context needs .as_ref().map(...) or .as_mut(), otherwise the original value is moved away.

Iterator adaptors are lazy and #[must_use]: a map chain without a consumer never runs (the compiler warns), and into_iter() moves the collection while iter() only borrows, which decides whether the closure may own its captures.
Err is never touched by Result::map (that is map_err), and a closure returning a Result nests the context - and_then is the flattening operation.
